s16.slug: SUNDAY · 4:30 PM → 5:30 PM · ST. CHARLES AVENUE NEAR NAPOLEON — THE FIRST THING
body: Every parade of the week has come down St. Charles Avenue, and the live oaks have kept a little of each. Beads hang in the branches as far up toward Napoleon and as far down toward town as Jack can see: purple and green and gold, a pink no tradition accounts for, strands gone gray from a year of weather and strands caught last night so high that nobody but the squirrels will ever get them down. The streetcar tracks lie idle down the middle of the neutral ground with the grass grown up between the ties. Clovis has backed his truck onto the grass with the tailgate down and Aints III on the tailgate in the quilted coat, and Tony’s ladder is chained to the hitch, and between the truck and the curb the Broussards have two blankets, a tarp, six folding chairs and the big cooler, and are defending them from Uptown, courteously, a yard at a time.

Uptown watches a parade in better coats. That was Lena’s ruling, delivered from the curb an hour ago, and the blankets round them bear it out: a man in a waxed jacket pouring something brown from a thermos into plastic cups, a grandmother in a camel coat with a plaid rug over her knees and a strand of purple beads over the camel, three little boys in matching corduroy fighting over one ladder. Across the avenue a big white house with columns has a speaker in its porch window, playing an old record with horns on it and a piano like a party falling down a flight of stairs, and a woman on the porch is dancing to it by herself with a drink in her hand. The light is draining out of the sky behind the oaks, and the cold is coming down to take its place.

Lena’s jean jacket has two pockets on the chest the size of playing cards, with buttons, for show. Somewhere between the truck and the curb her right hand went into the left pocket of his Carhartt, where his hand already was, and it’s there now. Her fingers were cold when they came in. They aren’t anymore. She talks across him to Tess about Lucille’s hat, which is a crocheted crawfish with antennae, and whether a crawfish is a respectful thing to put on a Catholic child for Bacchus, and in the pocket her fingers go through his to have somewhere to be.

On the tailgate beside the dog, Laney sees the pocket. She turns to Theo, and Theo has seen it too, and the two of them look up into the oaks together and study the beads up there as though they’d been assigned them for a test.
At five past five the RAZR goes off in the other pocket, the right one, where there’s nothing else but the tin. The lid says SKYE (MISFIT).

He takes his hand out of the pocket to answer it. Lena’s hand stays where it was without his for a moment, and then comes out, and goes to the cuff of her own jacket and takes hold of that instead. He steps back from the curb onto the streetcar tracks.
“Happy Valentine’s Day,” he says.

“I slept until noon,” says Skye. “Like a duchess. Like a cat in a window in Rome. I didn’t dream, I didn’t move, a maid came in at eleven and backed out again in terror. Happy Valentine’s Day, Jack.” The sleep is still in her voice, and under it the thing she sounds like when she has been waiting all day to dial.

body.text: “I opened it at six this morning,” she says. “In the lobby, in my coat, with the whole night still on me, standing at the front desk like a woman getting a telegram in a war picture. Because it was Sunday. I checked. The night man checked too. He went and found a calendar; he’s very thorough. And then I went upstairs and read your essay twice in my socks before I slept.”
“It’s O’Connor’s essay.”

“You sent it. That makes it yours. That’s how presents work, I looked it up.” He hears a page turn on her end. “She says it’s grace. The grandmother at the end, with her hand out. She says it right there in black and white, she practically underlines it for the slow kids in the back.” Another page. “And I still think the grandmother’s begging.” And then, slower, to herself as much as him: “Maybe begging’s allowed.”
“It’s allowed,” Jack says. “It’s about half the Psalms.”

“Don’t make it sound good. I’m trying to win.” She reads him the front of the book. She does it first as O’Connor herself, Milledgeville in every vowel, a woman who kept peacocks on principle; and then she reads it again in her own voice, slower, with nothing laid on it at all:

“*Mary Kate. It’s still nothing.*” She doesn’t read the rest. She doesn’t need the page for it; she was there the first time he said it, on a window seat in Montecito with her knees up. “That’s still the point,” Skye says.
“*Mary Kate. The hat was the point.*” She stops there, with the rest of it unread. “It was, too,” Skye says. “You were right about the hat. I hate it.”

“*For your margins. Strike anything you want.*” She makes a noise like a cat being offered a fish. “Strike anything I want. You’ll regret that. There’s a man in here from before you, Jack, with a pencil, and I have already struck him twice. He underlined *mystery* every single time it comes up, like it was going to be on the final.”

“*I’ve read you wrong too. I’m still reading.*” She says the last of it over, not reading now: “Still reading.” And after that she doesn’t say anything. Her thumb goes along the edges of the pages; he hears it, like a deck being riffled very slowly.

“They’re right here,” she says. “They called me in for a wig fitting on my one night off, which is a crime under Canadian law, and the violets are on the makeup counter between my script and Cassie’s wig, on its head, and I have been talking to them. In front of people. I read your card to the makeup lady and she cried, but she cries at the weather, so don’t get a big head.” Something rustles close to the phone: she has picked up the pot. “White violets. In February. In Burnaby.” And then low, delighted, as if she has caught him at something: “The *hat*.”
“In case of an accident,” Jack says, “so anybody seeing you dead on the highway would know.”
“That I was a *lady*. You remembered my bit.” He hears her set the pot back down, carefully, in exactly the place it was.

She reads him the card off the florist’s little envelope: “*Skye. For the hat. I’d cross the room again. Jack.*” She says the end of it over, without the card: “You’d cross the room again.” She doesn’t make a joke of it. She leaves it there.

She reads him the card: “*Skye. From the man on the porch, R-E colon* — the woman up here wrote it exactly like that, Jack, R-E colon, like you’re invoicing me — *your Colts fan.*” She is enjoying herself enormously. “The man on the porch, *regarding*. Kyle wants it framed. Kyle wants it on his headstone.”
She reads him the card: “*Skye. I miss you in daylight. J.*” And just the one word back, slow, turned over in her mouth: “In *daylight*.” He hears her sit down on the makeup chair.

body: “Okay, news,” Skye says. “Kyle bought a Saints shirt. At a gas station in Burnaby — don’t ask me where a gas station in Burnaby got a Saints shirt, there’s an underground — and he wears it under the Colts cap now, like a man with two families. The goose has seen it. The goose has views. Russ says changing teams after the game is the kind of thing that gets a man hosed down, and he’d know. He’s the one with the hose.”
“Kyle’s welcome down here,” Jack says. “They’d have him in a gold bag by Tuesday.”

“If you were in Burnaby,” she says, and her voice goes down to where she keeps it for the dark, “I wouldn’t be on the phone. I’d have you inside the door before your coat was off, and you wouldn’t see daylight till Tuesday.” And she laughs at herself, short and caught out. “Listen to me. On the Lord’s day.”

All through the call he has heard her moving: a floor that gives under her, a drawer, a chair dragged a foot, the rustle of something. Now there’s nothing. Wherever she is, she has stopped in the middle of it and is standing still.
“Nobody sends me the first thing,” Skye says. “They send the last thing. Flowers after the premiere.”
The woman on the porch across the avenue lifts the needle and the horns stop.
“You sent the first thing.”

He stands on the streetcar tracks with the phone to his ear and his other hand cold now, and he has nothing to say back to that which is good enough, and she doesn’t make him find it. The record starts over across the street.
“Did you go up this morning?” she says.

body.text: “Not this week.”
She has knelt beside him at St. Brendan’s. She knows what the pew means, and she knows what Wednesday was; he hears her sit down on whatever is nearest. “…Was it me?”
“It was me,” Jack says.
“Okay,” she says, very quietly. “Okay. Next week, then.”
“Not this week.”
“Not this week what?”
He tells her in one sentence: you don’t go up to Communion with something on you that you haven’t confessed, and he has something, and he hasn’t yet.
She takes that in. He hears her sit down. “…Was it me?”
“It was me,” Jack says.
“Okay,” she says, after a while. “Next week, then.”
“I went up.”
“Good,” Skye says, and then again, softer, to herself: “Good.”

body: She doesn’t ask where he is standing, or who with. She asks what time the king comes. “When he does,” she says, “hold your phone up for me. I want to see a king.”

Ten feet off, Lena is down at the curb with Josie, the two of them with their backs to him, watching the corner of Napoleon where the parade will turn. The bands haven’t come yet. The avenue is quiet enough to hear the porch speaker across it.

choices.text: “Love you, Mary Kate. Happy Valentine’s Day.”
choices.key: On Valentine’s Day, on St. Charles Avenue before Bacchus, Skye called about what you sent. You told her you love her, by her name.
response: “Love you, Mary Kate,” he says. “Happy Valentine’s Day.”
“Love you,” Skye says. She doesn’t make a bit out of the name. “Bye, Valentine.”
He folds the phone. At the curb Josie turns her head and looks at him over her shoulder. Lena goes on watching the corner of Napoleon.

choices.key: On Valentine’s Day, on St. Charles Avenue before Bacchus, Skye called about what you sent. You told her to hold on, there was a dinosaur.
response: Up at the corner of Napoleon, where the parade is gathering itself, something green and the size of a house swings round into the streetlight with its lights coming on one row at a time, all the way up to its teeth.
“Hold on,” Jack says. “There’s a dinosaur.”

“*Show* me,” Skye says, and he holds the RAZR out at arm’s length toward it, which shows her nothing, and she listens to it anyway, the whole avenue starting to holler at a dinosaur. “I heard it,” she says when he has the phone back. “It sounded expensive. Bye, Valentine.”

choices.key: On Valentine’s Day, on St. Charles Avenue before Bacchus, Skye called about what you sent. You told her you meant every word of it.
response: “I meant every word of it,” he says.
“I know,” Skye says. “That’s the problem with you.” But there’s nothing in it that’s a problem, and there’s the small sound of her picking the gift up again. “Bye, Valentine.”
The line goes. He stands on the tracks a little longer with the shut phone in his hand before he puts it away.

s16a.slug: SUNDAY · 5:40 PM → 6:40 PM · ST. CHARLES — THE KING
body: The picture comes in while the first band is still only a drum somewhere up Napoleon: *New Picture Msg*, and the RAZR takes its time with it, a stamp-sized square filling in from the top a band at a time, gray, then grain, then something he can make out if he tilts it to the streetlight.

body.text: She held the camera straight down over the hotel bed: his old flannel spread on the white sheet, and the book lying open on it to the front page, and his handwriting there, too small to read and he can read it anyway.
She held the camera straight down over the makeup counter: the pot of white violets in its green foil, and beside it the corner of a script gone soft at the edges from her hands.

body: He looks at it a long time, on the streetcar tracks, with Uptown going by him on both sides.
“Jack!” Lena has turned round at the curb with one arm up, loud, the voice she uses for floats. “*Band!*”

He puts the phone in his pocket and goes. The first band comes round the corner off Napoleon, a high school band in purple with a dance line in white boots and sequins and a drum major with a mace taller than Josie, and behind it the first float, lit end to end, and after that the avenue isn’t an avenue anymore. The floats come down under the oaks one after another out of the dark, every one of them burning, the riders masked in satin and throwing with both arms, and the beads come down out of the light in long ropes, and the oaks take half of them. A dinosaur float goes by, green, with its jaws working and a man in a mask riding on its back like he was born there. Tony is on the third rung of his ladder bellowing at riders by the color of their satin. Margot stands on the cooler for the view, arms folded, catching nothing on purpose. Kevin catches a plush Bacchus by its foot without looking and hands it to Lucille. Lena works the riders for Lucille tonight, only Lucille, and a man on a float full of masked wine gods hears “for the *baby*, sir, she’s eight weeks old and a Catholic” from the curb and lowers a plush bunch of grapes on a string all the way down into Tess’s lap.

Then, a long way up the avenue, a noise starts that Jack has heard once before, on Canal Street on Tuesday, and it comes toward them under the oaks the way weather comes in off the lake: it’s Canal, and then some. The king’s float comes out of the middle of it. Drew Brees rides high on it in the lights, in the crown and the robe, saluting the avenue with one arm and throwing with the other, and Uptown loses its better coats entirely.
Jack holds the RAZR up over the crowd as the float goes by and takes a picture of a king for a girl in Burnaby.

Something comes spinning out of the lights of the king’s float toward him, a long string of gold beads with a big medallion swinging at the end of it, and his hand goes up on its own — the reach of a Glenwood Avenue rec-league shortstop who never could hit but could always go to his left — and takes it out of the air one-handed.

The medallion is heavy and still warm from somebody’s hand: the god of wine in gold paint, with grapes in his hair. The curb has seen him catch it. Josie, in the box on top of the ladder, has her mouth open. Laney, by the truck, has her arms folded over her coat. Lena is at his elbow.

choices.key: At Bacchus you caught a medallion off the king’s float and put it in Lena’s hand.
response: He takes her hand and puts the medallion in it, beads and all.

Lena looks down at it. Her hand closes on it. She doesn’t put it on. She doesn’t give it back, or up the ladder to the twins, which is where everything she has caught all week has gone; she holds it in her shut fist against the front of her jean jacket and watches the parade with it there.
Beside the truck Laney turns round and walks straight off into the crowd on the neutral ground, and is gone a minute, and comes back with her face arranged.
Behind the king’s float the crowd surges toward the street, and Lena’s other hand, the empty one, comes looking for his and finds it.

choices.key: At Bacchus you caught a medallion off the king’s float and gave it to Laney for her birthday. Don’t, she said, and put it on.
response: He leans past Tony’s cooler and holds it out to her. “Happy birthday, Laney.”
Laney looks at the medallion, and at him, with the face she has kept for him in public since Christmas, a face like a closed store. “*Don’t*,” she says.

And she takes it, and puts it over her head, and lifts her hair out from under the beads with both hands, and doesn’t say anything else. Theo, next to her, stares hard after the dinosaur, a block gone up the avenue.
The crowd behind the king’s float leans forward all at once, and in the shove somebody’s hand takes his and holds it, and it’s Lena’s.

choices.key: At Bacchus you caught a medallion off the king’s float and put it over Josie’s head. Merci, she said.
response: He reaches up to the box on top of the ladder and puts the beads over Josie’s head, medallion and all, and settles it on her coat.
Josie, who keeps everybody’s secrets in this house and some of the neighbors’, looks down at him out of the box for a long second. “*Merci*,” she says.
Lena watches her sister take it in both hands and turn it to the light.
The surge behind the king’s float carries the curb forward a step, and Jack goes with it, and when it settles Lena’s hand is in his, and neither of them has let go of anything.

s17.slug: SUNDAY · 9:30 PM · DUPRE STREET, THE KITCHEN TABLE — NINETEEN CANDLES
body: They come in the back door at nine, beaded to the chin, Lucille asleep on Beau and Aints III asleep in Clovis’s arms, and the kitchen is dark. Laney is first through. “Y’all,” she says into the dark, the decree still in it, “I swear before God, if one single person —”
Celeste turns on the light.

On the oilcloth, on Grandmère’s cake stand, is a doberge: half chocolate and half lemon, down the middle like the flag of a very small country, nine layers thin as letters, the poured icing gone hard with her knife marks still in it. She must have made it this morning while they were out in the East. It has nineteen candles in it, out of the box Lena counted out on Friday.
Laney stops in the doorway with her hand still on the frame.
“Nobody did anything, baby,” Celeste whispers, going past her with the matches. “*I* did it.”

Julian’s roses are in the middle of the table in Grandmère’s cut-glass vase, right where the cake stand has to go. Tony comes round, picks up the vase in one hand, sets it on the windowsill over the sink, and comes back and puts the cake down where the roses were. Over the sink now there are a dozen red roses and the black window behind them, with the room reflected in it.

The whole kitchen is in the kitchen. Mémère has abandoned her lamp and her beads and come in on Remy’s arm to the chair at the end. Tess has Lucille handed back to Beau, who holds her like a football somebody wants. Clovis stands at the back door with the dog. The twins are on the piano bench, Josie in her school sweatshirt and Jude beside her.

body.text: Josie leans over and says *Destiny Thibodeaux* into her brother’s ear for no reason at all, and Jude goes red to the ears, the way he went at Endymion, and stays that way through the candles.
“He didn’t check *either* one,” Josie tells the table, of her brother, for no reason at all, and Jude looks at the ceiling fan.

body: Celeste seats the table like a ward round, in a whisper: Theo by the BlackBerry, Margot by Tess, Kevin at the corner where he can reach the milk. Jack she puts between Lena and Mémère without a word to either, and Mémère pats the oilcloth in front of his chair — “*Toi. Là.*” — in case he was thinking of sitting anywhere else. Kevin takes Theo’s iPhone out of the pocket of his windbreaker, where it has been since Thursday, and holds it out. “For the cake,” Kevin says. “*Only* the cake.” Theo takes it in both hands and photographs the cake: from above, from the side, the candles, the knife marks. He doesn’t point it at anything else in the room. He gives it back.

Laney’s pink BlackBerry is propped against the sugar shaker with Dallas on speaker, where the snow has her mother shut in, and Tammy Price is saying *Delaney Rose* every time anybody moves, and asking is it lit yet, and is Delaney Rose standing up straight. Lena leans down to the phone. “Miss Tammy, it’s Lena. She’s standing up straight. She looks beautiful. Mama made a doberge.” Out of Dallas, in a smaller voice: “Well. *Good*.” Celeste lights the candles. Somebody gets the light.

Lena starts the song, in a key she picks for everybody, and the kitchen comes in after her, badly: Tony a half step under, Remy somewhere over, Mémère in French, Margot audible and correct, Clovis a verse of his own. And out of the BlackBerry, half a bar behind all of them, comes Tammy, in a soprano that has been waiting all weekend for this. The kitchen finishes. Tammy doesn’t. She sings the last line alone out of the snow in Dallas, late, all the way to the end, and the kitchen waits for her.
Laney leans in. Sixteen candles go out in two breaths. Three stay lit at the far edge of the stand, and the twins lean over from the piano bench, one from each side, and get them.

Celeste puts the cake knife in Jack’s hand. “You cut, baby,” she whispers. “Thin. It’s nine layers, it’s not a brick.” So he cuts, under the eyes of three generations of Broussards and a speakerphone in Dallas, and Lena takes each plate off the knife as it comes and sends it on down the table — Mémère, Laney, Tony, the twins — and when Remy reaches across for a corner piece she raps his knuckles with the back of the server and goes on passing.

At the back door, in the dark blue of the NOPD with his radio turned low on his shoulder, Luc has ten minutes between Bacchus and the night, and he spends them on a slice on a paper plate, standing up, fast and with both hands, like a raccoon at a screen door. When the ten minutes are up he drops the plate in the trash, kisses his mother on the side of the head, touches the brim of his cap to the table in general and to Laney in particular, and goes back out to the night.

Then Tony stands up. He stands the way he stands at the eight o’clock to read the intentions, with his Abita in his hand, and the kitchen goes quiet for him, because when Tony stands up at a table it’s legislation.

“First time I ever heard this girl,” Tony says, “I was in that chair” — he points it out with the bottle, his own, at the end of the table, the cushion tied on — “and she was in a van in California, and I said, *put the redhead on*.”
Clovis laughs, and Remy, and Margot makes the noise she makes instead, and Laney laughs too, in spite of everything.

“In this house,” Tony says, “if you sleep under this roof on your birthday, you get a cake from Celeste and a toast from me, and you’re ours. That’s the rule.” He looks at the bottle in his hand. “I just made it.”
Laney puts both her hands on the oilcloth on either side of her plate. Her face goes, from the chin up, and she cries — at the table, in front of all of them, not hiding it in anything.

body.text: Jack thinks of the Delgado steps, and a pink cast that everybody signed.

body: The kitchen lets her. Lena, beside her, puts a hand on her back between the shoulder blades and leaves it there. Celeste comes round behind her chair and puts a hand on Laney’s hair, and then again. Across the table Theo looks at the cake as if it might go off.
Remy is moved. Remy is always moved; it’s the best thing about him. He gets to his feet with his glass up. “And to my brother-in —”
“*Remy*,” says Celeste.
Laney, still crying, reaches for the shaker on the oilcloth without looking and throws a pinch over her left shoulder. Theo takes it out of her hand across the table and throws some over his.
“Respectfully,” Kevin says, “that’s the sugar.”
“It’s the *thought*, Kevin,” Laney says, through it. “It *counts*.”
At the end of the table Mémère, who saw it go, crosses herself.

body.text: The king’s medallion is on Laney’s neck, where her collar opens, catching the kitchen light every time she breathes.
Lena’s right hand is on the oilcloth beside her plate, still shut. She has eaten her cake left-handed.
On the piano bench the king’s medallion hangs over Josie’s school sweatshirt, and she keeps one hand on it.

body: Lena, finished with hers, reaches over with her fork and takes the lemon end off Jack’s slice without asking, and he moves the plate over toward her so she can get at the rest. At the stove Celeste sees it, and looks at Tony, and Tony looks into the neck of his beer.
Laney lifts her head, and her wet eyes come across the cake and find Jack’s.

response: He holds out his paper napkin across the corner of the table.

response.text: “You have *got* to stop,” Laney says, wet, and takes it, and does her eyes with it, and keeps it balled in her fist on the oilcloth.
response.else: “Don’t,” Laney says, wet, and takes it, and does her eyes with it, and keeps it balled in her fist on the oilcloth.

response: “Nobody did anything,” Jack says.
Laney laughs, and it hurts her, and she picks up her fork and points it at him across the cake, tines first, like a woman with a lot to say who will be saying it later.
He looks at the cake: the knife marks, the nineteen black wicks, the line down the middle where chocolate meets lemon.
When he looks up again she is still looking at him. She has seen him not look. She nods, at the cake, and picks up her fork.

s18.slug: SUNDAY · 10:50 PM · THE BACK STEPS — THANK YOU FOR COMING
body: The yard is dark to the fence. The boil pot sits upside down on the picnic table like a bell somebody took down for the winter, the shed is a shape at the bottom of the yard with its line on it in the dark, and on the clothesline the gold bags hang where Celeste painted them, gone stiff in the cold and catching the light from the kitchen window.

body.text: LARGE, says the one nearest, in Celeste’s marker, turning a little on its clothespin.
body.else: One of them is big enough for nobody but Tony.

body: Two doors down, through somebody’s porch screen, a man on WWL is explaining to another man what’s wrong with the Hornets. He sits on the second step from the bottom with his elbows on his knees. Above him, in the yellow square of the kitchen window, are Julian’s roses.
He takes the RAZR out of the Carhartt, opens it, and finds the picture again: the gift, on her side of the mountains, grainier in the dark. He shuts it and puts it back in the pocket with the tin.
The screen door, and Lena, with the last of the cake on a saucer and two forks. She sits on the step above his, and her knee comes to rest against his shoulder.

body.text: The king’s medallion hangs out of one of the jean jacket’s useless pockets now, its beads looped twice round the button.

body: She gives him a fork. They eat off the one saucer, the lemon side, with the kitchen behind them going quiet a voice at a time: Tess saying goodnight, Beau and the diaper bag, the front door, Remy being told something about the dishes.
“Kevin will be hearing about the sugar till Easter,” Lena says.
“He was right.”
“He was *accurate*. In this family that’s a character flaw.” She eats a forkful of lemon. “Daddy made that rule up. The birthday one. He made it up standing there with a beer.”
“I know.”

“He’ll keep it now. He’ll keep it till they bury him. Every child who sleeps under this roof on a birthday, from now till the Second Coming, gets a doberge and a speech about a van.” She turns her fork over. “When’s yours?”
“March nineteenth.”
“Saint Joseph.” She considers that, chewing. “Daddy would build you an altar. Fava beans. Lemons. Mémère would make you bread in the shape of a beard.”
“I’ll be in California.”
“I know where you’ll be, Youngstown.”

Somebody’s sweet olive is over the fence, late in the year for it, and the cold keeps the smell low along the ground. There’s no moon. She cuts the last piece down to the last bite with the side of her fork and leaves it on the saucer, and through the window behind them the Magic Chef ticks.
“Jack,” she says, in the voice with nothing on it.
“Yeah.”
She lets out a breath. She starts again. Her fork is still in her hand, and she looks at the shed at the bottom of the yard, and then back down at him.
“Thank you for coming.”

choices.key: On the back steps after the cake, Lena said your name, and then thanked you for coming. You thanked her for having you.
response: “Thank you for having me,” he says.

Lena laughs once, wet, at being thanked like a hostess on her own back steps. She picks the last bite up on her fork and holds it out to him, and he takes the fork, and she gets up with the saucer and her knee leaves his shoulder.
The screen door claps to on its spring behind her. Over his head the window stays lit, with the roses in it.

choices.key: On the back steps after the cake, Lena said your name, and then thanked you for coming. You told her her mother says you’re a large.
response: “Your mother says I’m a large,” he says.

“You *are* a large.” She puts the last bite on her fork and hands him the fork, and while he eats it she stands, with a hand on his shoulder to do it, and takes the saucer up the steps past him and in.
The kitchen light lies out over the yard as far as the clothesline, and the roses stand up in the middle of it.

choices.key: On the back steps after the cake, Lena said your name, and then thanked you for coming. You took the fork she held out.
response: She has the last bite on her fork, held out to him. He takes it off her fork with his teeth.
Lena takes the fork back, and eats what’s left on it after him, the icing on the tines, without a word. She gathers the saucer and both forks and goes in by the kitchen door.
He sits on with his elbows on his knees and the yellow square over him, and the roses in it.

body: He goes in at half past eleven, through a kitchen put back together, past the cake stand under a dish towel, through the front room, where Mémère sleeps on the daybed with her beads slack in her fingers and her palms turned up on the blanket where Hébert put the oil on Thursday, and up the stairs, and up the ladder through the hatch.

The attic is dark but for the streetlight through the vent at the gable end, which lays a grille of orange over the rafters and the roofing nails coming through the deck overhead. Theo is asleep on the air mattress with his back to the room, or doing it well. Kevin lies by the hatch on his back, awake, turning a red envelope over in his fingers in the orange light, the one the Phạm grandmother gave him at the table.
Jack lies down under Remy’s Tiger poster in the sleeping bag. In the Carhartt, on the floor beside him, the RAZR goes.

body.text: clear. 9

body: Thursday it was six. He looks at the nine a while by the light of the little screen. He answers her, short, with his thumb, and shuts the phone, and lays it on his chest.
“Tomorrow I’m nineteen,” Kevin says, to the rafters.
Jack comes up on an elbow. “Kevin. Why didn’t you say?”
“It was Laney’s day.”

Kevin turns the envelope over once more and puts it away inside his windbreaker and zips the pocket. After a minute, still to the rafters: “Bà Nội says I came on the first morning of the Goat.” He doesn’t say anything else, and Jack lies back down.

body.text: Hébert’s penance was done this morning, on his fingers, kneeling after Communion. Tonight, under the nails, he says one more Hail Mary for her anyway, that nobody asked him for, with *Mary Kate* in the middle of it.
When he shuts his eyes the card from the vestibule at Holy Rosary is there on the inside of the lids, white, in its frame — CONFESSIONS · SATURDAY · 3:00–4:00 P.M. — and he opens them again.
He says the words off the medal at the tomb, once, under his breath: *O Mary, conceived without sin, pray for us who have recourse to thee.*

body: Across the attic Theo breathes like a sleeping man. Kevin is quiet. The box fan stands dead in the gable window with the streetlight coming through its blades, and Jack lies on his back with the phone on his chest and the nails over him, every one of them with a point of orange on it, and his eyes open.
